column2: A limit on how long a session may last after sign-in, however active it is; the app sets it to 12 hours.
A path that starts from the top of the file system, such as `/c/dev/secure-doc-viewer`, and so means the same wherever you are.
An AWS tool that reports which resources, such as buckets, can be reached from outside your account.
A Java keyword (`public`, `private`, package-private) that decides who may use a class, field or method.
In a threat model, a person or program that can interact with the system, such as a reader, a publisher or an attacker.
The Spring Boot library that adds operational endpoints such as health checks and metrics.
A design pattern in which a small class translates one interface into the one your code expects.
The role that may manage users, sessions and the audit log, and see every document; in code, `ADMIN`.
The AWS content delivery network, which serves files from locations near the reader.
The AWS service that collects logs and metrics from ECS and the load balancer and raises alarms.
Elastic Container Registry, the AWS registry that stores container images.
Elastic Container Service, the AWS service that runs containers.
An AWS-managed in-memory store (Valkey or Redis OSS) that all tasks can share.
An AWS service that starts a task or another target on a schedule.
An AWS-managed store that accepts Prometheus metrics, so you do not run a Prometheus server yourself.
Relational Database Service: AWS runs a database such as MySQL for you, including patching, backups and failover.
The AWS DNS service.
Simple Storage Service: AWS object storage that keeps files (objects) by key in buckets, with no real directories and no atomic folder rename.
The framework, written in TypeScript, in which the app's browser side is built from components, services and routes.
The `ng` command-line program that creates, serves, builds and tests an Angular project.
A label starting with `@` that you attach to Java code so that a framework or the compiler can read it.
Spring's container: the object that creates, holds and connects all of the application's beans.
An AWS service that receives HTTPS requests, spreads them over healthy tasks and health-checks each one.
A named, large-scale shape for arranging a whole system, such as layers, a gateway or an event log.
A value you give to a command or to a method call so that it knows what to act on.
The unique address of one AWS resource, such as a secret or a role.
A short way to write a function in JavaScript and TypeScript, using `=>`.
In a threat model, something worth protecting, such as the documents, the signing secret or the accounts.
Describes a step that happens completely or not at all, so that nothing else can see it half done.
The persisted record of who did what and when, which administrators can search and export; the audit trail is its content.
The permanent, append-only record of important actions such as sign-ins, uploads, views and denied requests, kept so that events can be investigated later.
Proving who you are, for example with a username and password.
Deciding what an authenticated person is allowed to do.
Spring Boot's habit of setting up sensible defaults for the libraries it finds on the classpath.
One or more separate data centers inside an AWS Region; using two means a failure in one does not take you down.
An AWS service that schedules and manages backups and restores of databases and storage.
The AWS service that issues public TLS certificates and renews them.
A way to run ECS containers without managing servers.
The AWS service that stores secrets and can inject them into a container as environment variables at start.
A web application firewall that attaches rules to a load balancer or a CloudFront distribution.
A library that scans a rendered page for accessibility problems, such as low contrast or missing labels.
The part of an application that runs on a server and holds the data and the rules.
A password-hashing function that is deliberately slow and reads at most 72 bytes of the password.
An object that Spring creates and manages, from a class labeled with an annotation such as `@Service`.
The Java standard for declaring input rules with annotations such as `@NotBlank` and `@Size`.
Java's automatic conversion between a primitive value such as `int` and its object form such as `Integer`.
A movable name for a line of work in Git.
The program, such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari or Edge, that requests web pages and runs their code.
The sequence of steps that turns source code into a tested, packaged program.
The folder that Docker sends to the builder when you build an image.
A program that compiles code, runs tests and packages the result; Maven is the one this project uses for Java.
A design pattern that gives each kind of work its own limit, so that overload in one does not sink the rest.
The compact instructions that the Java compiler produces and the JVM runs.
A place where a copy of something is kept so that it can be served again faster.
A naming style with no spaces in which each word after the first starts with a capital letter, such as `tileCount`.
The fixed, unambiguous text that is signed when a tile token is made: the payload fields joined in a set order.
A URL whose possession is what lets you fetch the one thing it names; a signed tile URL is an example.
A network of servers around the world that keeps copies of files near readers so that they load quickly.
Division that rounds up, used to count how many tiles are needed to cover a page.
A signed statement, issued by an authority the browser trusts, that a public key belongs to a given domain.
An organization that browsers trust to issue certificates.
A design pattern in which a request passes along a line of handlers, each of which may handle it, change it or pass it on.
Angular's process of deciding which parts of the screen to redraw when data changes.
A Java exception, such as `IOException`, that a method must catch or declare with `throws`.
The practice of running tests and checks automatically on every proposed change.
A compact way to write a range of network addresses, such as `10.0.0.0/16`.
A named blueprint in Java that describes the data and the behavior of a kind of object.
An attack that hides a real page inside a frame on a hostile page so that you click on it without knowing.
A program that asks for things over a network; your browser is a client.
To copy an existing Git repository, with its history, to your machine.
The practice of having someone else read a change before it is merged.
A Java object that holds many values, such as a list, a set or a map.
A text interface in which you type commands to the computer; see terminal.
A saved state in Git: a snapshot of every tracked file at one moment, with a message and a unique identifier.
The long hexadecimal identifier that uniquely names a Git commit.
A program that checks source code and translates it into a form that a machine can run.
A message from the compiler that stops the build before anything runs.
Spring's search of your packages for annotated classes to register as beans.
A primary key made of more than one column, such as a document and a user together.
Building a class by giving it other objects to use, instead of inheriting from another class.
An Angular signal whose value is calculated from other signals and recalculated only when they change.
Several things happening at overlapping times, for example many requests handled by many threads.
The `condition ? a : b` form, which gives `a` when the condition is true and `b` otherwise.
A check whose running time does not depend on how many characters match, so that an attacker cannot learn a secret from timing.
A rule that a database enforces on a column or table, such as `NOT NULL` or `UNIQUE`.
Special code that runs when you create an object with `new` and sets up its fields.
Dependency injection in which an object receives its dependencies as constructor parameters.
A running, isolated instance of an image: a program packaged with everything it needs.
A response header that tells the browser which sources a page may load scripts, images and connections from.
The difference in brightness between text and its background, measured as a ratio.
A class that receives web requests and returns responses.
The design habit of choosing sensible defaults so that you configure only what differs; Maven and Spring Boot both follow it.
A small piece of data that a server asks the browser to store and send back with later requests.
The browser mechanism by which a server says which other origins may read its responses.
The three values (group, artifact and version) that identify a Maven project or library.
The processor that does a computer's calculations.
A compact schedule with fields for second, minute, hour, day, month and weekday, such as `0 30 3 * * *`.
An attack in which another website makes your browser send a request to a site where you are signed in.
A secret value that the app's own page sends back in a header on every change, so that a forged request cannot supply it.
An attack in which a spreadsheet cell that starts with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` runs as a formula when an exported CSV file is opened.
A public identifier, in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list, for one known security flaw in some software.
A small class, often a record, that carries exactly the data of one request or response.
A program that stores an application's data permanently and lets you query it.
A small file that expands to a huge amount of data or pixels when processed, exhausting memory.
An address that leads straight to a specific state, such as the viewer at page 3 of a document.
Whatever stands in the way of a threat.
The principle of layering several independent protections so that one failure does not expose everything.
An attack, or a side effect, that makes a service unavailable to the people who need it.
Storing a copy of information in more than one place instead of linking to one copy.
A stance in which anything not explicitly allowed is refused.
A GitHub service that opens pull requests when newer versions of your dependencies exist.
A library that your code uses.
Giving an object the other objects it needs instead of letting it create them itself.
Turning text or bytes, such as JSON, back into an object.
A named, reusable solution to a problem that recurs in code.
The inspection panel built into browsers that shows requests, code and errors.
The empty angle brackets `<>` in Java, which tell the compiler to work out the type arguments from the left-hand side.
A fingerprint of exact contents, such as the SHA-256 hash that identifies one Docker image.
A TypeScript union of object types that each carry a fixed tag field, so that code can tell them apart.
The internet's phone book, which turns a name such as `docs.example.com` into a network address.
The tool that builds and runs programs in containers.
A tool that describes several containers in one file, `docker-compose.yml`, and starts them with one command.
The recipe of steps that builds a Docker image.
A `/** ... */` comment that documents a class or method for people and for documentation tools.
A CSRF defense in which the same value arrives twice, once in a cookie and once in a header that only the real page can set.
How many pixels represent one inch of a page when it is rendered as an image.
Hibernate's habit of noticing that a loaded entity was changed and saving the change when the transaction ends.
Hiding a class's fields and exposing only the operations you intend.
The rule that maps characters to bytes; the project's files use UTF-8.
Scrambling data with a key so that only someone with the key can read it.
A test that drives the whole running application through a real browser.
A Java class whose objects are stored as rows in a database table.
A Java type that lists all the allowed values of a small fixed set, such as the roles.
A named setting, such as `DB_PASSWORD`, that the operating system hands to every program it starts.
A time written as the number of seconds since January 1, 1970, UTC.
An ordered record of things that happened, added to and never edited.
A design in which the sequence of events is the source of truth and the current state is derived from it.
An object that signals that something went wrong and interrupts normal flow until it is handled.
A method that turns a particular exception into a controlled HTTP response.
One file that holds the application, its libraries and the web server, so that a single command starts the whole application.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt, for example 50, 100, 200 and 400 milliseconds.
A design pattern in which one small, simple interface stands in front of a larger subsystem.
A static method that builds an object, so that callers need not know how.
Refusing a bad situation at the first opportunity instead of letting it travel further into the code.
A Git merge that simply moves a branch pointer forward because no other changes exist.
Prepared sample data or state that a test starts from.
An option that changes how a command behaves, such as `-l` in `ls -l`.
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any change to the code.
A CSS layout mode, `display: flex`, that arranges children in a row or column and spaces them.
A style in which each method returns the object itself so that calls chain into one readable sentence.
A tool that applies numbered SQL migration files to a database in order.
A container for files and other folders; also called a directory.
A column that holds the primary key of a row in another table, linking the two.
A large body of ready-made code that supplies the structure of an application and calls your code at the right moments.
The part of an application that runs in the user's browser.
A reverse proxy at the edge that does more than forward requests, for example applying common rules to all of them.
A Java or TypeScript type that is written with a placeholder, such as `List<String>`, so that one definition works for many types.
A method that reads a private field of an object.
The version control tool that records every change to the project's files.
The terminal that comes with Git for Windows and understands the bash commands used in this book.
Stopping a server by refusing new requests and letting the ones in progress finish first.
A check at the top of a method that returns or throws at once when a precondition is not met.
A fixed-length, one-way fingerprint of data.
The library that maps Java objects to database tables; it is the JPA implementation this project uses.
A keyed hash: a short code that only someone holding the secret key can compute, used to detect tampering.
The folder where your personal files live; `~` is shorthand for it.
The computer that runs Docker and its containers.
A response header that tells browsers to use only HTTPS for a site from then on.
The set of rules that browsers and servers use to exchange requests and responses.
HTTP carried inside an encrypted channel created by TLS.
A set of permissions that a program assumes temporarily in AWS, with no stored password or key.
Describes an operation that has the same effect when done twice as when done once.
What a cloud resource bills while it exists, whether or not anyone uses it.
The time a session may sit unused before it ends; the app sets it to 30 minutes.
A read-only template from which Docker containers are started.
Describes something that cannot change after it is created.
A Java statement that lets you use a class from another package by its short name.
A sorted lookup structure on one or more database columns, so that matching rows are found without reading the whole table.
Describing servers, networks and other infrastructure in files that can be reviewed, versioned and re-applied.
Building a new class by taking everything an existing class has and adding to it.
A single point on the timeline, independent of time zones; `Instant` is the Java class for it.
A test that starts several pieces together, for example the real security filters and a real controller.
A function in Angular's HTTP client that sees every request and response, used for the CSRF header and for reacting to `401`.
A description of what an object can do (Java) or of its shape (TypeScript), without saying how.
Inserting the value of an expression into text in an Angular template with `{{ }}`.
The principle that a framework, not your code, creates objects and decides when to call them.
The number that identifies a computer on a network, such as `203.0.113.9`.
The Java library that converts between objects and JSON.
A Java Archive: a zip file of compiled classes.
The programming language that browsers run.
The Java Development Kit: the compiler and tools needed to build Java programs.
A query operation that combines rows from two tables.
A table that holds pairs of keys to link two other tables in a many-to-many relationship.
The Jakarta Persistence standard for mapping Java objects to database tables.
The JPA query language, which talks about classes and fields instead of tables and columns.
The Java Runtime Environment: the part of Java needed only to run programs, without the compiler.
A pretend browser written in JavaScript, so that tests can create page elements without a real browser.
A text format for structured data made of objects, lists, strings, numbers and booleans.
A JSON Web Token: a signed piece of text that carries claims and can be verified without a server-side session.
The Java Virtual Machine: the program that runs compiled Java.
The AWS service that creates and holds encryption keys.
A small unnamed method that you can pass around.
A counter that makes threads wait until it reaches zero; tests use it to release parallel threads at once.
In Docker, one step of an image build, stored once and reused; in architecture, a level of code that may call only the level below it.
An arrangement in which code is divided into levels, such as controllers, services and repositories, each calling only the one below.
Loading related data only when it is first used.
The principle of giving a process or person only the access it needs.
A collection of ready-made code that your program calls when it needs it.
A method that Angular calls when a component appears or is removed, such as `ngOnInit`.
An S3 rule that expires old object versions or aborts incomplete uploads after a set time.
The mark that ends a line of text: Windows uses two bytes (carriage return and line feed), macOS and Linux use one (line feed).
A Java collection that keeps items in order and allows duplicates.
A value written directly in code, such as `512` or `"hello"`.
The name a computer uses for itself; requests to it never leave the machine.
The stream of text lines that a running program writes to say what it is doing.
A release line that receives fixes for years, which the project prefers for MySQL, Node and Java.
A small script that Redis runs atomically, so that several commands take effect as one.
A short, recognizable byte pattern at the start of a file that shows its type, such as `%PDF-`.
A service in which the provider runs the software for you, including patches and backups, and you give up some control.
A relationship in which each row on one side can link to many on the other and the reverse; it needs a join table.
A Java collection of key and value pairs, looked up by key.
The build tool this project uses to compile, test and package its Java code.
The public online repository from which Maven downloads libraries.
A small script (`mvnw`) that downloads and runs the exact Maven version the project uses.
Combining the changes of one Git branch into another.
A commit that joins two lines of work and has two parents.
A stop in a merge because two branches changed the same lines and Git cannot choose.
A named block of code that does one job and can be called by name.
A short form of a lambda that only calls one method, such as `AppUser::getUsername`.
A number that a running program exposes over time, such as how many tiles it has served.
The Java library that collects metrics and hands them to a system such as Prometheus.
A design in which each part of a system is its own separately deployed program that talks to the others over the network.
A versioned change to a database schema, applied once and in order.
A stand-in object that records how it was called, used to test code without its real collaborators.
A single deployable program whose inside is divided into modules with clear responsibilities.
A file or group of code that exports some things and imports others.
A Dockerfile that builds in one stage and copies only the result into a small final image.
The request format that carries files and form fields together, used for uploads.
A setup that keeps a synchronous standby copy in a second Availability Zone and fails over automatically.
A viewer that only hides its download button in the browser, so that anyone can still fetch the file.
An AWS service that lets resources in private subnets reach the internet; it bills while it exists.
A program that runs JavaScript outside a browser, on your own computer.
Running a program as an ordinary user instead of the all-powerful root user, so that a break-in does less harm.
Node's package manager, which downloads libraries from a public registry.
One thing built from a class, with its own values for the fields.
How well you can tell what a running system is doing from what it reports.
A design pattern in which a publisher announces events and any number of subscribers react.
A flaw in which a site sends the browser to whatever address a link names, so that an attacker can dress a hostile link as a trusted one.
A way for one service, such as GitHub, to prove its identity to another, such as AWS, and receive short-lived credentials with no stored key.
A symbol such as `+` or `==` that combines or compares values.
A Java object that is either empty or holds one value, used instead of `null`.
The combination of scheme, host and port that browsers use to decide who may read whose responses.
A library that translates between objects in code and rows in a database.
Open Source Vulnerabilities: a database of published security advisories, used to check the project's dependencies.
The account that uploaded a document and may manage it.
A Java folder-like namespace that groups related classes.
A named input that a method declares; the values passed in are its arguments.
A Maven project file that other projects inherit defaults from, such as a tested list of library versions.
How Java passes arguments: the method receives a copy of a primitive value.
The address of a file or folder, written with slashes between folder names.
The environment variable that lists the folders a shell searches for commands.
Portable Document Format: a file type that describes pages so that they look the same everywhere.
A tool that drives a real browser, used for the end-to-end tests.
An image file format that stores a grid of pixels without losing detail.
Restoring a database to any moment within a retention period.
A numbered door on a computer, from 0 to 65535, at which a server listens for network requests.
An S3 URL that grants temporary access to one object to whoever holds it.
A column, or set of columns, whose value identifies each row uniquely.
A running program.
A named set of extra Spring settings switched on for a purpose, such as the test profile.
A list of instructions that a computer follows.
A system that collects metrics by fetching a web page from each program at a regular interval.
The query language for Prometheus metrics.
A JavaScript object that stands for one result that will arrive later or fail.
The text a shell shows to say that it is ready for your next command.
A `${NAME:default}` marker in configuration that Spring replaces with an environment or file value.
An agreed format for a conversation between programs, such as HTTP.
A program that receives a request on behalf of another server and forwards it.
The role that may upload documents and manage its own; in code, `PUBLISHER`.
A proposal on GitHub to merge one branch into another, with a place for discussion and review.
A repository method whose name Spring turns into a database query.
The part of a URL after the `?`, which carries small pieces of data.
A bug in which the result depends on the timing of things that happen at once.
To turn a page description, such as a PDF page, into a grid of pixels.
A cap on how many requests a user may make in a period.
The role that may open the documents shared with it; in code, `READER`.
A compact Java class for immutable plain data.
A network address from which an account has signed in successfully in the last 30 days, which the sign-in throttle treats more leniently.
Three questions for watching a service: the Rate of requests, the Errors and the Duration.
Sending a command's output somewhere other than the screen, such as into a file.
A geographic area where AWS runs data centers.
A test written so that a fixed bug cannot come back unnoticed.
A database that stores data in tables linked by keys.
A path that starts from the folder you are in.
Spring's rule that `signing-secret`, `SIGNING_SECRET` and `signingSecret` all name the same setting.
A copy of a Git repository on another computer, usually on GitHub.
A Git project (files plus the hidden `.git` folder that holds history), or in Spring a class that reads and writes one kind of entity.
The data a client sends with a request, such as the JSON of a form.
A word that SQL reserves for its own use, so that it cannot be used as a plain column name.
A thing that a REST API exposes at a URL, such as a document.
A named value, such as `Cache-Control`, that a server sends before the body of a response.
A style of web API built around URLs for things and HTTP methods for actions.
How long backups, logs or records are kept before they are deleted.
A server that sits in front of an application, receives requests from browsers and passes them on.
A named set of permissions attached to an account, such as reader, publisher or administrator.
To undo every change of a transaction because it failed.
A function that Angular runs before it lets a user into a route, used for a better experience and never as security.
A database lock on selected rows, so that two transactions cannot change them at once.
How much recent data you can afford to lose, expressed as time.
How long a restore may take before the outage is unacceptable.
An error that happens while the program runs rather than while it compiles.
A bucket setting that keeps earlier versions of an object so that an overwritten or deleted object can be recovered.
Random data mixed into a password before hashing, so that equal passwords produce different hashes.
The browser rule that a script from one origin may not freely read responses from another.
A cookie setting that limits when the browser sends the cookie on requests that start from another site.
The set of tables and columns of a database.
A Maven setting that says when a dependency is needed, such as only for tests.
Fetching a program's metrics page, which is how Prometheus collects data.
Replacing a secret with a new one on a schedule or after a leak.
Describes software whose safe setting is the one you get if you configure nothing.
A firewall attached to an AWS resource that says which traffic may enter and leave.
A counter of permits that limits how many threads may do something at once.
Turning an object into text or bytes, such as JSON, so that it can be sent or stored.
The program that answers requests from clients; here, the Spring Boot app.

A layer of services that keeps the rules in one place, so that two controllers cannot apply them differently.
Code that every web request passes through before it reaches a controller.

A helper container that runs beside the main container in the same task.
An Angular value that remembers who has read it and tells them when it changes.
A value computed from data and a secret key that proves the data was not changed.
A URL carrying a signature that the server can verify, so that it cannot be altered or forged.

The human-readable text of a program, before it is compiled.

A web app that loads once and then draws its screens in the browser, asking the server only for data.
The framework that starts the server and connects the application's classes with sensible defaults.
The Spring library that writes common database queries from repository interfaces.
The Spring library that handles sign-in, sessions, roles and request protection.
The language used to query and change a relational database.
An attack that smuggles SQL commands into an input so that the database runs them.
The list of method calls that were active when an exception occurred, printed to help find the cause.
In Git, the place where changes wait until you commit them.
A single dependency that pulls in a matched set of libraries for one purpose, such as `spring-boot-starter-security`.
A design that names the possible states and the allowed moves between them.
A static method, such as `Viewer.of(...)`, that returns a new object.
The three-digit number in a response that says what happened, such as `404`.
A Java pipeline that processes a collection step by step, filtering, transforming and collecting.
A sequence of characters; text.
A design pattern in which interchangeable pieces of behavior are chosen at run time.
A stand-in with just enough behavior for a test.
A division of a VPC's addresses; a private subnet has no route from the internet.
The libraries and images your software depends on, which other people wrote.
A set of rows in a relational database, with named columns.
A permanent name for one Git commit, like a bookmark.

A design pattern in which a fixed skeleton is written once and the caller supplies the variable step.
A window in which you type commands to the computer instead of clicking.
Code that checks other code.

A file that holds characters rather than, say, an image.
A path of execution inside a program; a web server handles many requests at once on many threads.
A specific way someone might misuse the system.
A structured description of a system's assets, actors, entry points and threats.
Limiting how many attempts are allowed in a period.
One small square piece of a rendered page image.

A group of database statements that all succeed or all fail.

The line between what a system controls, such as the server, and what it does not, such as the browser.

A label that says what kind of value something is.
JavaScript with a type system that a compiler checks before the code runs.
A Java exception that the compiler does not force you to catch.
A TypeScript type that allows one of several listed alternatives.

A database write that inserts a row or, if one exists, updates it.

Discovering which usernames exist from differences in how a service answers.

The common encoding that stores each character in one to four bytes.
A universally unique identifier: a long random-looking value, such as a document's id.
An open-source, Redis-compatible in-memory store.
A small immutable object defined by its values, with no identity of its own.
A named place that holds a value.
A tool that records every change to a project's files so that you can return to any earlier state.
A whole computer simulated by software, which is heavier than a container.
Whether a document is private (owner, administrators and shared users) or open to everyone.
The test runner used for the frontend's unit tests.

Your own private network inside AWS, divided into subnets.

Text or a mark drawn onto content to identify who received it.
